@sec-tissue-mechanics showed how soft brain tissue is. How does a cell read that? One route runs through ion channels opened by membrane stretch, above all Piezo1. In *Xenopus* embryos, blocking or knocking down Piezo1 disrupts optic tract growth [@koser2016mechanosensing, Fig. 5]; in rat oligodendrocyte progenitors, Piezo1 transmits the stiffening of the ageing niche [@segel2019niche, Fig. 3]. A second route, through adhesions and the cytoskeleton, needs no channel.

::: {.callout-note title="After this chapter you will be able to"}
- describe how Piezo1 was discovered and state its basic properties (non-selective cation channel, $E_\mathrm{rev}$ about +6 mV, ~23 pS);
- distinguish "force-from-lipid" from tether gating, with a scale of membrane tensions;
- explain why reported Piezo1 parameters differ between studies;
- contrast the channel route with the adhesion–actomyosin–YAP/TAZ route, and name the tools used to probe each.
:::

## Mechanosensitive channels {#sec-piezo-channels}

**Mechanotransduction** is "the conversion of mechanical force into biological signals" [@coste2010piezo, Introduction]. **Mechanosensitive ion channels** are pore-forming membrane proteins that respond to mechanical stimuli "by changing the opening probability of their pore" [@pillai2024mechanics, p. 9]. Many brain channels are mechanosensitive, from TRAAK and TREK1 to NMDA receptors [@tyler2012mechanobiology, Table 1], but most also respond to chemical signals, pH or temperature; Piezo channels "exclusively respond to mechanical signals" [@pillai2024mechanics, p. 10].

## The discovery of Piezo1 {#sec-piezo-discovery}

@coste2010piezo searched for the molecules behind **mechanically activated (MA) currents** in four steps:

1. **Choose a cell.** Of seven mouse and rat cell lines, Neuro2A (N2A) mouse neuroblastoma cells had the most consistent MA currents [@coste2010piezo, sec. "Neuro2A cells express MA currents"].
2. **List candidates.** Transcripts enriched in N2A cells, filtered for proteins predicted to cross the membrane at least twice [@coste2010piezo, sec. "Piezo1 (Fam38A) is required for MA currents of N2A cells"].
3. **Knock down each one.** siRNA against *Fam38A* abolished the MA currents. The gene was renamed Piezo1, from the Greek for pressure (same section).
4. **Overexpress.** Mouse Piezo1 or Piezo2 increased MA currents 17- to 300-fold in several cell types [@coste2010piezo, Discussion].

In a **poke**, a glass probe indents the cell during whole-cell recording; in **stretch**, pipette suction pulls on a cell-attached patch [@coste2010piezo, sec. "Neuro2A cells express MA currents"]. Poking is "very qualitative": the force on the channel is unknown [@brohawn2014mechanosensitivity, Discussion].

Piezo1 currents reverse near +6 mV and pass Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, "with a slight preference for Ca²⁺"; Gd³⁺ and ruthenium red (30 µM) block them [@coste2010piezo, sec. "Piezo1 induces MA currents in various cell types"]. Piezo2, cloned from mouse dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, inactivates faster (about 7 ms at −80 mV) and is required for their rapidly adapting MA currents [@coste2010piezo, Fig. 5–6].

## Force from lipid, or from tethers? {#sec-piezo-gating}

There are two gating models [@brohawn2014mechanosensitivity, Introduction]. In **force-from-lipid** gating, tension in the bilayer itself favours the open state. In **tether** gating, force reaches the channel through attached cytoskeletal or extracellular-matrix proteins. Brohawn and colleagues reconstituted the purified K⁺ channels TRAAK and TREK1 in pure lipid; stretch still opened them, so no tether was needed [@brohawn2014mechanosensitivity, sec. "Biophysical Origins of Mechanosensitivity in TRAAK and TREK1"].

For scale: an unpressurised patch already carries ~0.5–4 mN/m of tension, and the bacterial channels MscS and MscL begin to open at ~5 and ~9 mN/m [@brohawn2014mechanosensitivity, Discussion]. Mechanical channels can oppose each other: in N2A cells, added TRAAK turned the Piezo1-driven depolarisation into a small biphasic response [@brohawn2014mechanosensitivity, Fig. 1].

Piezo1 is "largely thought to be activated by an increase in membrane tension", consistent with force-from-lipid [@pillai2024mechanics, p. 10; @nourse2022piezo, Discussion]. Its sensitivity and inactivation are tuned by membrane cholesterol and fatty acids [@nourse2022piezo, Discussion]. Yet on stiffer substrates Piezo1 activity rises while axonal membrane tension does not, and how Piezo1 is activated in vivo is unknown [@pillai2024mechanics, pp. 10–11].

Why do the values differ?

- **Cell type.** Suction on cell-attached patches gave P50 of −28 to −31 mmHg in N2A and HEK293T cells [@coste2010piezo, Fig. 1F, 4H, 4K] but −13.4 mmHg in human fetal neural stem/progenitor cells (NSPCs) [@pathak2014stretch, Fig. 1D].
- **Salt and preparation.** About 23 pS in a cell-attached N2A patch [@coste2010piezo, Fig. 1D]; 98 pS for purified Piezo1 in a bilayer in 0.5 M KCl at +100 mV, with Yoda1 [@syeda2015chemical, Fig. 3B].
- **Stimulus.** P50 exists only for suction; poking is graded by probe displacement [@coste2010piezo, sec. "Neuro2A cells express MA currents"].
- **Drugs.** Yoda1 lowered P50 by about 15 mmHg [@syeda2015chemical, p. 4].

## Tools to activate and block Piezo1 {#sec-piezo-tools}

**Yoda1** came from a screen of about 3.25 million compounds with a fluorescent Ca²⁺ readout on a FLIPR plate reader (@sec-indicators) [@syeda2015chemical, p. 8]. It activates mouse and human Piezo1 but not Piezo2, slows inactivation, and opens purified Piezo1 in lipid bilayers with no other proteins present [@syeda2015chemical, pp. 2–7]. Its apparent EC50 (17–27 µM) is unreliable because Yoda1 becomes insoluble above ~20 µM [@syeda2015chemical, pp. 3–4]. Jedi1 and Jedi2 are further Piezo1 agonists; none exists for Piezo2, and agonists should be applied only briefly [@pillai2024mechanics, p. 11]. Inhibitors (Gd³⁺, ruthenium red, the tarantula peptide GsMTx4) are non-specific and mostly act by altering membrane mechanics [@pillai2024mechanics, p. 11], so genetic knockdown is the usual specificity control.

## Two routes from stiffness to the nucleus {#sec-piezo-routes}

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-piezo-routes
%%| fig-cap: "**Schematic, not data.** Two routes of mechanotransduction. Top: a channel route (tens of ms; Pillai & Franze 2024, p. 10) from membrane tension through Piezo1 to Ca²⁺ influx. Bottom: an adhesion route (YAP/TAZ relocate within ~2 h; Dupont et al. 2011, p. 181) through focal adhesions and actomyosin tension to YAP/TAZ. Dashed links were shown in human fetal NSPCs (Pathak et al. 2014). Schematic, not exhaustive."
flowchart LR
  S["Matrix stiffness"]
  T["Membrane tension"] --> P["Piezo1 opens"] --> C["Ca²⁺ and Na⁺ influx"]
  A["Focal adhesions"] --> M["Actomyosin tension<br/>(Rho, myosin II)"] --> Y["YAP/TAZ in nucleus"]
  S --> T
  S --> A
  M -. "traction" .-> P
  P -. "knockdown: Yap leaves nucleus" .-> Y
  C --> F["Gene expression, fate, growth"]
  Y --> F
```

Matrix sensing requires a cell to "pull against the matrix" and a transducer that reports the force needed [@engler2006matrix, p. 677]. Human mesenchymal stem cells on brain-like gels (0.1–1 kPa) became branched and expressed neuronal markers, and blocking non-muscle myosin II with blebbistatin abolished this lineage choice [@engler2006matrix, Figs. 1, 3]. Downstream, the transcriptional coactivators **YAP and TAZ** were nuclear on stiff (15–40 kPa) and cytoplasmic on soft (0.7–1 kPa) gels in cultured human cells. This required Rho and actomyosin tension, but not the Hippo kinases LATS1/2 [@dupont2011role, pp. 179–181].

The routes meet in human fetal NSPCs (23 weeks' gestation). There, myosin II traction opened Piezo1 without external force, giving local Ca²⁺ "hotspots" that were minimal on 0.4–0.7 kPa and larger on stiffer substrates [@pathak2014stretch, sec. "Piezo1 Is Activated by Traction Forces"]. Piezo1 knockdown pushed Yap out of the nucleus, and blocking Piezo1 shifted differentiation from neurons to astrocytes [@pathak2014stretch, Figs. 4–5].

The schematic below walks through that experiment. Pick a substrate, or one of the three perturbations Pathak and colleagues tested on glass, and watch which link of the chain breaks.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import { PIEZO_CONDITIONS, channelOpen } from "../js/piezo-states.js"
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof pzCond = Inputs.radio(new Map(PIEZO_CONDITIONS.map(c => [c.label, c])), {
  value: PIEZO_CONDITIONS[4], label: "Condition"
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: fig-piezo-traction
//| fig-cap: "**Schematic, not data; conditions and outcomes from @pathak2014stretch.** Human fetal neural stem/progenitor cells (23 weeks' gestation) imaged with the Ca²⁺ dye Fluo-4 by TIRF microscopy. Myosin II pulls on actin fibres (lines), and the pull reaches the substrate through focal adhesions (dots), as traction (arrows) [sec. \"Piezo1 Is Activated by Traction Forces\"]. Piezo1 channels (triangles) in the basal membrane let Ca²⁺ in, which gives local Ca²⁺ \"hotspots\" (glow). Outcomes: minimal or no transients on 0.4 and 0.7 kPa, increasing activity on 3.7 kPa, 750 kPa and glass [Fig. 4C–D]; abolished by 6 mM EGTA [Fig. 3C–D] and by 50 µM blebbistatin [Fig. 4A–B]; fewer and smaller after Piezo1 siRNA [Fig. 3E–F]. The perturbations were tested on glass and are shown only there. Not from the literature: the glow brightness is an ordinal rank built from the authors' words, not a measured amplitude, and the open or closed state of each drawn channel is our reading of the outcome; nothing is to scale."
{
  const c = pzCond
  const W = Math.min(width, 640), H = 300
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", [0, 0, W, H]).attr("width", W).attr("height", H)
    .attr("role", "img").attr("aria-label", `Piezo1 schematic: ${c.label}`)
  const ySub = 230, x0 = W * 0.18, x1 = W * 0.82
  // Substrate: darker = stiffer (ordinal).
  svg.append("rect").attr("x", 0).attr("y", ySub).attr("width", W).attr("height", H - ySub)
    .attr("fill", "#9aa5b1").attr("fill-opacity", 0.15 + 0.6 * c.stiffness)
  svg.append("text").attr("x", 10).attr("y", H - 12).attr("fill", "currentColor").attr("font-size", 12)
    .text(`substrate: ${c.label.split(" + ")[0]}`)
  // Bath Ca²⁺ (removed by EGTA).
  if (c.calciumOutside) {
    for (let i = 0; i < 9; i++) {
      const x = 30 + i * (W - 60) / 8, y = 30 + (i % 3) * 14
      svg.append("circle").attr("cx", x).attr("cy", y).attr("r", 3.5).attr("fill", "#eda100")
    }
    svg.append("text").attr("x", W - 12).attr("y", 24).attr("text-anchor", "end").attr("fill", "currentColor").attr("font-size", 12).text("Ca²⁺ in the bath")
  } else {
    svg.append("text").attr("x", W - 12).attr("y", 24).attr("text-anchor", "end").attr("fill", "currentColor").attr("font-size", 12).text("bath Ca²⁺ chelated by EGTA")
  }
  // Cell body.
  svg.append("path")
    .attr("d", `M${x0},${ySub} C${x0},${ySub - 120} ${x1},${ySub - 120} ${x1},${ySub} Z`)
    .attr("fill", "#2a78d6").attr("fill-opacity", 0.12).attr("stroke", "#2a78d6").attr("stroke-width", 2)
  // Ca²⁺ hotspot glow near the basal membrane.
  const glow = svg.append("defs").append("radialGradient").attr("id", "pz-glow")
  glow.append("stop").attr("offset", "0%").attr("stop-color", "#eda100").attr("stop-opacity", 0.95)
  glow.append("stop").attr("offset", "100%").attr("stop-color", "#eda100").attr("stop-opacity", 0)
  const chX = [0.35, 0.5, 0.65].map(f => x0 + f * (x1 - x0)).slice(0, c.channels === 3 ? 3 : 1)
  const open = channelOpen(c)
  for (const x of chX) {
    if (c.level > 0) svg.append("ellipse").attr("cx", x).attr("cy", ySub - 14).attr("rx", 18 + 40 * c.level).attr("ry", 10 + 26 * c.level)
      .attr("fill", "url(#pz-glow)").attr("opacity", 0.25 + 0.75 * c.level)
    const g = open ? 7 : 0
    svg.append("path").attr("d", `M${x - 12 - g},${ySub + 2} L${x - 2 - g},${ySub - 16} L${x - 2 - g},${ySub + 2} Z`).attr("fill", "#8e5ed6")
    svg.append("path").attr("d", `M${x + 12 + g},${ySub + 2} L${x + 2 + g},${ySub - 16} L${x + 2 + g},${ySub + 2} Z`).attr("fill", "#8e5ed6")
  }
  if (c.channels < 3) svg.append("text").attr("x", (x0 + x1) / 2).attr("y", ySub + 22).attr("text-anchor", "middle")
    .attr("fill", "currentColor").attr("font-size", 12).text("fewer Piezo1 channels (siRNA)")
  // Actin fibres with focal adhesions, and traction arrows.
  for (const [xa, xb] of [[x0 + 20, x0 + 0.45 * (x1 - x0)], [x1 - 20, x1 - 0.45 * (x1 - x0)]]) {
    svg.append("line").attr("x1", xa).attr("y1", ySub - 4).attr("x2", xb).attr("y2", ySub - 70)
      .attr("stroke", c.traction ? "#e34948" : "#9aa5b1").attr("stroke-width", 3).attr("stroke-dasharray", c.traction ? null : "4,4")
    svg.append("circle").attr("cx", xa).attr("cy", ySub - 2).attr("r", 5).attr("fill", "currentColor")
    if (c.traction) {
      const d = xa < W / 2 ? 1 : -1
      svg.append("path").attr("d", `M${xa - d * 30},${ySub + 14} L${xa + d * 10},${ySub + 14} M${xa + d * 2},${ySub + 8} L${xa + d * 10},${ySub + 14} L${xa + d * 2},${ySub + 20}`)
        .attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#e34948").attr("stroke-width", 2.5)
    }
  }
  svg.append("text").attr("x", (x0 + x1) / 2).attr("y", ySub - 100).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "currentColor").attr("font-size", 12)
    .text(c.traction ? "myosin II pulls on actin" : "myosin II blocked (blebbistatin)")
  return html`<div>${svg.node()}<p class="source-note"><strong>${c.label}.</strong> ${c.note} (Pathak et al. 2014, ${c.cite})</p></div>`
}
```

Things to try:

- Step from 0.4 kPa to glass: the hotspots appear and grow with substrate stiffness, although nothing pushes or pulls on the cell from outside.
- Choose blebbistatin: the channels and the bath Ca²⁺ are still there, but without the cell's own pull the hotspots vanish. Choose EGTA: the pull is there, but there is no Ca²⁺ to let in.

::: {.callout-warning title="Species matter"}
Human fetal NSPCs made more neurons on stiff substrates, opposite to rodent NSCs [@pathak2014stretch, sec. "Effect of Substrate Stiffness on hNSPC Differentiation"]. In mouse NSCs from *Piezo1* knockout embryos at E10.5, astrocyte *and* neuron differentiation fell [@nourse2022piezo, Fig. 3B]; the authors attribute the conflict to species or knockdown versus knockout [@nourse2022piezo, Discussion]. @sec-frontier returns to these results.
:::

## Check yourself {#sec-piezo-check}

:::{.qmulti correct="4"}
Coste et al. report about 23 pS for Piezo1, and Syeda et al. 98 pS. What best explains the difference?

- Yoda1 widens the open pore, so each channel passes more current.

  > Yoda1 acts mainly by stabilising the open state: the mean open time rose from 13 to 55 ms [@syeda2015chemical, pp. 4–7]. The two recordings also differ in preparation and salt [@syeda2015chemical, Fig. 3B].

- Coste et al. recorded human Piezo1, and Syeda et al. mouse Piezo1.

  > Both recorded mouse Piezo1: endogenous channels in mouse Neuro2A cells [@coste2010piezo, Fig. 1D] and purified mouse Piezo1 [@syeda2015chemical, Fig. 3B].

- The N2A patches also contained Piezo2, which has a smaller conductance.

  > Knocking down Piezo1 alone abolished the MA currents of N2A cells [@coste2010piezo, sec. "Piezo1 (Fam38A) is required for MA currents of N2A cells"], so the N2A channels are Piezo1.

- One used purified channel in 0.5 M KCl, the other an intact N2A mouse cell.

  > Correct. Coste et al. recorded cell-attached patches on N2A cells [@coste2010piezo, Fig. 1D]; Syeda et al. recorded purified Piezo1 in a lipid bilayer in 0.5 M KCl at +100 mV, with 1 µM Yoda1 [@syeda2015chemical, Fig. 3B].

:::

:::{.qmulti correct="4"}
Purified TRAAK in pure lipid still opens when stretched. What does this show?

- TRAAK needs tethers to the cytoskeleton to open.

  > The preparation had no cytoskeleton: purified TRAAK was reconstituted in lipid alone, and stretch still opened it [@brohawn2014mechanosensitivity, sec. "Biophysical Origins of Mechanosensitivity in TRAAK and TREK1"].

- Piezo1 in the same membrane pulls TRAAK open.

  > The purified system held TRAAK and lipid, and no Piezo1, so Piezo1 cannot explain the opening.

- Piezo1 is therefore gated by bilayer tension as well.

  > The experiment tested TRAAK and TREK1, not Piezo1. Piezo1 is thought to sense membrane tension, but how it is activated in vivo is unknown [@pillai2024mechanics, pp. 10–11].

- Tension in the bilayer is enough to gate TRAAK.

  > Correct. Purified TRAAK and TREK1 in pure lipid opened when stretched, so no tether was needed: this is force-from-lipid gating [@brohawn2014mechanosensitivity, sec. "Biophysical Origins of Mechanosensitivity in TRAAK and TREK1"].

:::

**Compute.** A patch at the upper estimate of resting tension (4 mN/m) needs at least {{< qinput 5 tol=0.5 hints="MscL begins to open at ~9 mN/m" >}} mN/m more tension to reach the threshold of MscL.

:::{.qmulti correct="3"}
A paper blocks Piezo1 with GsMTx4. What control would you ask for?

- A higher dose of GsMTx4, to block Piezo1 more fully.

  > More drug does not make GsMTx4 more specific: it is non-specific and mostly acts by altering membrane mechanics [@pillai2024mechanics, p. 11].

- Yoda1 treatment, to show that the cells express Piezo1.

  > Yoda1 activates Piezo1 [@syeda2015chemical, pp. 2–7], so it shows that the channel is present, not that GsMTx4 acted through it.

- Piezo1 knockdown, to show the effect needs Piezo1.

  > Correct. GsMTx4 is non-specific [@pillai2024mechanics, p. 11]; removing Piezo1 genetically tests whether the effect depends on the channel.

- Gd³⁺ or ruthenium red, as a second Piezo1 blocker.

  > Gd³⁺ and ruthenium red are non-specific too and also act mostly by altering membrane mechanics [@pillai2024mechanics, p. 11].

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answers" collapse="true"}
1. Preparation and salt: a patch on an intact N2A cell versus purified channel in a bilayer in 0.5 M KCl [@coste2010piezo, Fig. 1D; @syeda2015chemical, Fig. 3B].
2. Bilayer tension is enough to gate TRAAK: force from lipid [@brohawn2014mechanosensitivity, sec. "Biophysical Origins of Mechanosensitivity in TRAAK and TREK1"].
3. 9 − 4 = 5 mN/m; resting patches carry ~0.5–4 mN/m and MscL opens at ~9 mN/m [@brohawn2014mechanosensitivity, Discussion].
4. Piezo1 knockdown (or knockout), because GsMTx4 is non-specific [@pillai2024mechanics, p. 11; @pathak2014stretch].
:::

## Summary {#sec-piezo-summary}

- Piezo1, found by an siRNA screen in N2A cells, is a non-selective cation channel reversing near +6 mV [@coste2010piezo].
- Force-from-lipid gating was shown directly for TRAAK and TREK1; Piezo1 is thought to sense membrane tension, but in vivo activation is unclear [@brohawn2014mechanosensitivity; @pillai2024mechanics, pp. 10–11].
- Piezo1 parameters depend on cell type, stimulus, salts and drugs: P50 −13 to −31 mmHg, conductance 23 to 98 pS [@coste2010piezo; @pathak2014stretch; @syeda2015chemical].
- Stiffness is also read via adhesions, myosin II and YAP/TAZ; human NSPCs link both routes [@engler2006matrix; @dupont2011role; @pathak2014stretch].

:::{.qflashcards}

- What makes Piezo channels convenient for mechanobiology?

  > They respond only to mechanical signals, unlike TRP or K2P channels.

- What does Yoda1 do?

  > It activates Piezo1 (not Piezo2), lowers P50 and slows inactivation.

- Where are YAP/TAZ on soft substrates?

  > In the cytoplasm (inactive); on stiff ones they are nuclear.

- Name a Piezo1 inhibitor and its problem.

  > GsMTx4; it is not specific.

:::
